claim: Ventral tegmental area (VTA) activity is critical for reward/reinforcement.
source: Ventral tegmental area (VTA) activity is critical for reward/reinforcement and is tightly modulated by the laterodorsal tegmentum (LDT).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about VTA function.

claim: VTA activity is tightly modulated by the laterodorsal tegmentum (LDT).
source: Ventral tegmental area (VTA) activity is critical for reward/reinforcement and is tightly modulated by the laterodorsal tegmentum (LDT).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact.

claim: In utero exposure to glucocorticoids (iuGC) triggers prominent motivation deficits.
source: In utero exposure to glucocorticoids (iuGC) triggers prominent motivation deficits but nothing is known about the impact of this exposure in the LDT-VTA circuit.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known finding.

claim: iuGC-rats have long-lasting changes in cholinergic markers in the LDT.
source: We show that iuGC-rats have long-lasting changes in cholinergic markers in the LDT, together with a decrease in LDT basal neuronal activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: iuGC-rats have a decrease in LDT basal neuronal activity.
source: We show that iuGC-rats have long-lasting changes in cholinergic markers in the LDT, together with a decrease in LDT basal neuronal activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 2b.

claim: Upon LDT stimulation, iuGC animals present a decrease in the magnitude of excitation in the VTA.
source: Interestingly, upon LDT stimulation, iuGC animals present a decrease in the magnitude of excitation and an increase in VTA inhibition, as a result of a shift in the type of cells that respond to the stimulus.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 2k.

claim: Upon LDT stimulation, iuGC animals present an increase in VTA inhibition.
source: Interestingly, upon LDT stimulation, iuGC animals present a decrease in the magnitude of excitation and an increase in VTA inhibition, as a result of a shift in the type of cells that respond to the stimulus.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 2o.

claim: The changes in VTA responses to LDT stimulation in iuGC animals result from a shift in the type of cells that respond to the stimulus.
source: Interestingly, upon LDT stimulation, iuGC animals present a decrease in the magnitude of excitation and an increase in VTA inhibition, as a result of a shift in the type of cells that respond to the stimulus.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2h showing different proportions of putative dopaminergic and GABAergic neurons responding.

claim: iuGC animals present motivational deficits that are rescued by selective optogenetic activation of the LDT-VTA pathway.
source: In agreement with LDT-VTA dysfunction, we show that iuGC animals present motivational deficits that are rescued by selective optogenetic activation of this pathway.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by behavioral data in Figure 4a.

claim: LDT-VTA optogenetic stimulation is reinforcing.
source: Importantly, we also show that LDT-VTA optogenetic stimulation is reinforcing, and that iuGC animals are more susceptible to the reinforcing properties of LDT-VTA stimulation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by CPP and RTPP data in Figure 4.

claim: iuGC animals are more susceptible to the reinforcing properties of LDT-VTA stimulation.
source: Importantly, we also show that LDT-VTA optogenetic stimulation is reinforcing, and that iuGC animals are more susceptible to the reinforcing properties of LDT-VTA stimulation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by CPP data in Figure 4e-f showing that lower stimulation induces preference in iuGC but not control animals.

claim: The VTA comprises dopaminergic (~65%), GABAergic (~30%), and glutamatergic neurons (~5%).
source: The VTA comprises dopaminergic (~65%), GABAergic (~30%), and glutamatergic neurons (~5%) (Nair-Roberts et al., 2008; Yamaguchi et al., 2011) that receive inputs from diverse brain regions, including the laterodorsal tegmentum (LDT) (Woolf and Butcher, 1986; Cornwall et al., 1990; Oakman et al., 1995; Oakman et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The VTA receives inputs from diverse brain regions, including the laterodorsal tegmentum (LDT).
source: The VTA comprises dopaminergic (~65%), GABAergic (~30%), and glutamatergic neurons (~5%) (Nair-Roberts et al., 2008; Yamaguchi et al., 2011) that receive inputs from diverse brain regions, including the laterodorsal tegmentum (LDT) (Woolf and Butcher, 1986; Cornwall et al., 1990; Oakman et al., 1995; Oakman et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Exposure to unexpected rewards can activate VTA dopaminergic neurons culminating in the release of dopamine in the nucleus accumbens (NAc).
source: Several studies have shown that exposure to unexpected rewards, or cues that predict rewards, can activate VTA dopaminergic neurons culminating in the release of dopamine in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) (Roitman et al., 2004; Stuber et al., 2005; Stuber et al., 2008; Schultz et al., 1997; Bromberg-Martin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Cues that predict rewards can activate VTA dopaminergic neurons culminating in the release of dopamine in the nucleus accumbens (NAc).
source: Several studies have shown that exposure to unexpected rewards, or cues that predict rewards, can activate VTA dopaminergic neurons culminating in the release of dopamine in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) (Roitman et al., 2004; Stuber et al., 2005; Stuber et al., 2008; Schultz et al., 1997; Bromberg-Martin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: VTA dopaminergic neuron activity is tightly modulated by cholinergic projections.
source: Importantly, this activity is tightly modulated by cholinergic projections (Omelchenko and Sesack, 2005; Omelchenko and Sesack, 2006), with an additional contribution of glutamatergic projections, arising from the LDT (Cornwall et al., 1990; Oakman et al., 1999; Lammel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Glutamatergic projections from the LDT contribute to VTA dopaminergic neuron activity.
source: Importantly, this activity is tightly modulated by cholinergic projections (Omelchenko and Sesack, 2005; Omelchenko and Sesack, 2006), with an additional contribution of glutamatergic projections, arising from the LDT (Cornwall et al., 1990; Oakman et al., 1999; Lammel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: LDT input is vital for the activity of dopaminergic cells in the VTA.
source: This input is vital for the activity of dopaminergic cells in the VTA, facilitating dopamine-related behaviors involved in reward signaling or encoding reward prediction signals (Lodge and Grace, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of LDT neurons that project to the VTA enhances conditioned place preference.
source: In agreement, recent studies have shown that optogenetic stimulation of LDT neurons that project to the VTA enhances conditioned place preference (Lammel et al., 2012) and operant responses in rodents (Steidl and Veverka, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of LDT neurons that project to the VTA enhances operant responses in rodents.
source: In agreement, recent studies have shown that optogenetic stimulation of LDT neurons that project to the VTA enhances conditioned place preference (Lammel et al., 2012) and operant responses in rodents (Steidl and Veverka, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The mesolimbic system is particularly vulnerable to the effects of prenatal stress/high levels of glucocorticoids.
source: Notably, different labs have shown that the mesolimbic system is particularly vulnerable to the effects of prenatal stress/high levels of glucocorticoids (GCs) (Matthews, 2000; Boksa and El-Khodor, 2003; McArthur et al., 2005; Leão et al., 2007; Rodrigues et al., 2011; Borges et al., 2013a; Soares-Cunha et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Prenatal stress/high levels of glucocorticoids may increase the risk to develop neuropsychiatric disorders in adulthood, namely depression, anxiety and addiction.
source: These changes may increase the risk to develop different neuropsychiatric disorders in adulthood, namely depression, anxiety and addiction (Seckl, 2008; Rodrigues et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: GCs can induce acetylcholine release.
source: This is particularly intriguing because GCs can induce acetylcholine release (Finkelstein et al., 1985; Gilad et al., 1985; Imperato et al., 1989) and bind to GC-responsive elements of cholinergic enzymes, namely choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) and acetylcholine esterase (AChE) to control their expression (Berse and Blusztajn, 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: GCs bind to GC-responsive elements of choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) to control its expression.
source: This is particularly intriguing because GCs can induce acetylcholine release (Finkelstein et al., 1985; Gilad et al., 1985; Imperato et al., 1989) and bind to GC-responsive elements of cholinergic enzymes, namely choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) and acetylcholine esterase (AChE) to control their expression (Berse and Blusztajn, 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: GCs bind to GC-responsive elements of acetylcholine esterase (AChE) to control its expression.
source: This is particularly intriguing because GCs can induce acetylcholine release (Finkelstein et al., 1985; Gilad et al., 1985; Imperato et al., 1989) and bind to GC-responsive elements of cholinergic enzymes, namely choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) and acetylcholine esterase (AChE) to control their expression (Berse and Blusztajn, 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Stress changes cholinergic enzymes expression.
source: In fact, it has been shown that stress changes cholinergic enzymes expression (Finkelstein et al., 1985; Kaufer et al., 1998), either by inducing an alternative splicing of AChE gene (Nijholt et al., 2004), or by modulating the epigenetic status of its promoter regions (Sailaja et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Prenatal GC exposure induces a long-lasting hyperanxious state associated with an increase in the recruitment of cholinergic cells from the LDT.
source: In accordance, we have previously shown that prenatal GC exposure induces a long-lasting hyperanxious state associated with an increase in the recruitment of cholinergic cells from the LDT (Borges et al., 2013b), suggesting that GCs are able to program the LDT, which prompted us to evaluate the impact of prenatal GC in the LDT-VTA circuitry and its impact in reward-related behaviors.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: iuGC animals had a significant increase in the density of the cholinergic population of the LDT at 30 days of age.
source: iuGC animals had a significant increase in the density of the cholinergic population of the LDT at 30 days of age (post-hoc Bonferroni; CTR(30 days) vs. iuGC(30 days): t(25) = 2.616, p=0.0446) that persisted until adulthood (post-hoc Bonferroni; CTR(90 days) vs. iuGC(90 days): t(25) = 3.971, p=0.0016).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The increase in the density of the cholinergic population of the LDT in iuGC animals persisted until adulthood.
source: iuGC animals had a significant increase in the density of the cholinergic population of the LDT at 30 days of age (post-hoc Bonferroni; CTR(30 days) vs. iuGC(30 days): t(25) = 2.616, p=0.0446) that persisted until adulthood (post-hoc Bonferroni; CTR(90 days) vs. iuGC(90 days): t(25) = 3.971, p=0.0016).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Other brain regions containing cholinergic neurons such as the nucleus basalis of Meynert or the NAc remained unaltered in iuGC animals.
source: Other brain regions containing cholinergic neurons such as the nucleus basalis of Meynert or the NAc remained unaltered (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: ChAT gene expression levels were increased at 3 and 30 days of age in iuGC animals.
source: ChAT gene expression levels were increased at 3 and 30 days of age in iuGC animals (Figure 1d; post-hoc Bonferroni; CTR(3 days) vs. iuGC(3 days): t(24) = 3.383, p=0.0074; CTR(30 days) vs. iuGC(30 days): t(24) = 3.053, p=0.0164; CTR(90 days) vs. iuGC(90 days): t(24) = 2.494, p=0.059).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Decreased AChE gene expression levels were found in adult iuGC animals.
source: Decreased AChE levels were found in adult iuGC animals (Figure 1e; post-hoc Bonferroni; CTR(3 days) vs. iuGC(3 days): t(23) = 1.24, p=0.6827; CTR(30 days) vs. iuGC(30 days): t(23) = 2.244, p=0.1043; CTR(90 days) vs. iuGC(90 days): t(23) = 3.298, p=0.0094).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1e.

claim: VAChT mRNA levels were unchanged between groups in the LDT.
source: We also evaluated the levels of another cholinergic marker, the vesicular acetylcholine transporter (VAChT) and found that mRNA levels were unchanged between groups in the LDT (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Western blot analysis confirmed the upregulation of ChAT in the iuGC group at all ages tested.
source: Western blot analysis confirmed the upregulation of ChAT (Figure 1f–g; post-hoc Bonferroni; CTR(3 days) vs. iuGC(3 days): t(23) = 4.401, p=0.0006; CTR(30 days) vs. iuGC(30 days): t(23) = 2.762, p=0.0333; CTR(90 days) vs. iuGC(90 days): t(23) = 2.712, p=0.0373); and downregulation of AChE in the iuGC group at all ages tested (Figure 1f and h; post-hoc Bonferroni; CTR(3 days) vs. iuGC(3 days): t(18) = 4.73, p=0.0005; CTR(30 days) vs. iuGC(30 days): t(18) = 3.157, p=0.0164; post-hoc Bonferroni CTR(90 days) vs. iuGC(90 days): t(18) = 3.349, p=0.0107).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1f-g.

claim: Western blot analysis confirmed the downregulation of AChE in the iuGC group at all ages tested.
source: Western blot analysis confirmed the upregulation of ChAT (Figure 1f–g; post-hoc Bonferroni; CTR(3 days) vs. iuGC(3 days): t(23) = 4.401, p=0.0006; CTR(30 days) vs. iuGC(30 days): t(23) = 2.762, p=0.0333; CTR(90 days) vs. iuGC(90 days): t(23) = 2.712, p=0.0373); and downregulation of AChE in the iuGC group at all ages tested (Figure 1f and h; post-hoc Bonferroni; CTR(3 days) vs. iuGC(3 days): t(18) = 4.73, p=0.0005; CTR(30 days) vs. iuGC(30 days): t(18) = 3.157, p=0.0164; post-hoc Bonferroni CTR(90 days) vs. iuGC(90 days): t(18) = 3.349, p=0.0107).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1f,h.

claim: Gene and protein expression levels of glutamate transporter EAAC1 were not significantly affected by iuGC exposure.
source: Gene and protein expression levels of glutamate transporter EAAC1 and GAD1/67 + GAD2/65 were not significantly affected by iuGC exposure.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Gene and protein expression levels of GAD1/67 + GAD2/65 were not significantly affected by iuGC exposure.
source: Gene and protein expression levels of glutamate transporter EAAC1 and GAD1/67 + GAD2/65 were not significantly affected by iuGC exposure.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: No differences were found between groups regarding GR expression.
source: We found no differences between groups regarding GR expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 3d,h).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3d,h.

claim: iuGC animals presented a VTA-NAc hypodopaminergic state.
source: Previous work from our group showed that iuGC animals presented a VTA-NAc hypodopaminergic state (Leão et al., 2007; Borges et al., 2013a; Soares-Cunha et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the results with supporting citations from previous work.

claim: The LDT innervates the VTA and can influence NAc dopamine release.
source: Since the LDT innervates the VTA and can influence NAc dopamine release (Blaha and Winn, 1993; Blaha et al., 1996; Forster and Blaha, 2000; Forster et al., 2002; Miller et al., 2002; Forster and Blaha, 2003), we decided to characterize the LDT-VTA circuit using in vivo single cell electrophysiology in anesthetized animals (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results with supporting citations.

claim: iuGC treatment significantly decreased the spontaneous activity of LDT neurons.
source: iuGC treatment significantly decreased the spontaneous activity of LDT neurons (Figure 2a–b; t(128) = 4.674, p<0.0001, total number of cells: CTR = 36, iuGC = 94; nCTR = 8, niuGC = 11 animals).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2b.

claim: No differences were found in the basal activity of VTA between control and iuGC animals.
source: No differences were found in the basal activity of VTA (Figure 2c–d; t(70) = 0.0576, p=0.9542, total number of cells: CTR = 40, iuGC = 32; animals: CTR = 8, iuGC = 11).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Electrical stimulation at 0.5 Hz of the LDT evoked both excitatory and inhibitory responses in VTA neurons in contrasting percentages between control and iuGC animals.
source: Electrical stimulation at 0.5 Hz of the LDT evoked both excitatory and inhibitory responses in VTA neurons in contrasting percentages (Figure 2e; CTR: 50% excitatory and 30% inhibitory; iuGC: 31% excitatory and 44% inhibitory).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2e.

claim: iuGC animals present a shift in the type of neurons that present excitatory responses, with an increase in pGABAergic neurons and concomitant decrease in pDAergic neurons.
source: Interestingly, iuGC animals present a shift in the type of neurons that present excitatory responses, with an increase in pGABAergic neurons and concomitant decrease in pDAergic neurons. Excitatory responses were observed in 70% of pDAergic and 20% of pGABAergic neurons in CTR animals versus 30% of pDAergic and 60% of pGABAergic neurons in iuGC animals.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2h.

claim: The iuGC group presented an increase in pDAergic neurons showing inhibitory responses together with a decrease in pGABAergic neurons showing inhibitory responses.
source: Regarding inhibition, the iuGC group presented an increase in pDAergic neurons together with a decrease in pGABAergic neurons (Figure 2h). Briefly, inhibitory responses were observed in 21% of pDAergic and 50% of pGABAergic neurons in CTR animals versus 57% of pDAergic and 28% of pGABAergic neurons in iuGC animals.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2h.

claim: The onset of excitation in VTA neurons upon LDT electrical stimulation was significantly increased in iuGC group in comparison to control group.
source: The onset of excitation was significantly increased in iuGC group in comparison to control group (Figure 2j; CTR: 0.45 ± 0.114 ms vs. iuGC: 9.33 ± 2.49 ms; t(30) = 4.637, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2j.

claim: iuGC treatment reduced the magnitude of the excitatory response in VTA neurons upon LDT electrical stimulation.
source: Interestingly, iuGC treatment reduced the magnitude and duration of the excitatory response (Figure 2k–l; magnitude: t(30) = 3.723, p=0.0008; duration: t(30) = 2.196, p=0.0360).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2k.

claim: iuGC treatment reduced the duration of the excitatory response in VTA neurons upon LDT electrical stimulation.
source: Interestingly, iuGC treatment reduced the magnitude and duration of the excitatory response (Figure 2k–l; magnitude: t(30) = 3.723, p=0.0008; duration: t(30) = 2.196, p=0.0360).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2l.

claim: The response magnitude of inhibitory responses in the VTA evoked by LDT electrical stimulation was significantly higher in iuGC animals.
source: However, the response magnitude of inhibitory responses in the VTA evoked by LDT electrical stimulation was significantly higher in iuGC animals (Figure 2o; t(28) = 2.905, p=0.0071).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2o.

claim: The WGA–Cre fusion protein is retrogradely transported.
source: The WGA–Cre fusion protein is retrogradely transported (Gradinaru et al., 2010), inducing the expression of cre-dependent ChR2-YFP only in LDT neurons that directly project to the VTA (Figure 3a–c).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of LDT terminals in the VTA (30 pulses of 15 ms at 20 Hz) increases the firing rate of VTA neurons in both control and iuGC groups.
source: As depicted in Figure 3d, optogenetic stimulation of LDT terminals (30 pulses of 15 ms at 20 Hz) induced an increase in firing rate of VTA neurons (Figure 3d, post-hoc Bonferroni test CTR-ChR2: baseline vs. stimulus - t(118) = 5.883, p<0.0001, stimulus vs. post-stimulus - t(118) = 3.749, p=0.0008; iuGC-ChR2: baseline vs. stimulus - t(118) = 10.99, p<0.0001; stimulus vs. post-stimulus - t(118) = 10.88, p<0.0001), eliciting a response in 69% and 71% of recorded cells of CTR and iuGC animals, respectively (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3d.

claim: In CTR animals, 49% of VTA cells presented increased firing rate upon LDT terminal stimulation, and of these, 69% were pDAergic, 17% pGABAergic and 14% were categorized as 'other' neuronal subtypes.
source: In CTR animals, 49% of cells presented increased firing rate upon stimulation, and of these, 69% were pDAergic, 17% pGABAergic and 14% were categorized as 'other' neuronal subtypes.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3g.

claim: In CTR animals, 87% of VTA cells that presented inhibitory responses to LDT terminal stimulation were pGABAergic neurons.
source: Moreover, 87% of cells that presented inhibitory responses were pGABAergic neurons (Figure 3f–g).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3g.

claim: In iuGC animals, 44% of VTA cells presented increased firing rate upon LDT terminal stimulation, and the majority were pDAergic neurons (83%).
source: In iuGC animals, 44% of cells presented increased firing rate upon stimulation, and the majority were pDAergic neurons (83%).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3g.

claim: In iuGC animals, 55% of VTA cells that presented inhibitory responses to LDT terminal stimulation were pDAergic neurons and 36% were considered to be pGABAergic neurons.
source: Surprisingly, and clearly different from CTR animals, 55% of cells that presented inhibitory responses were pDAergic neurons and 36% were considered to be pGABAergic neurons (Figure 3g).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3g.

claim: iuGC-ChR2 rats presented a significant decrease in breakpoint in comparison to CTR, CTR-YFP and CTR-ChR2 animals in the progressive ratio test.
source: In the test day, iuGC-ChR2 rats presented a significant decrease in breakpoint in comparison to CTR, CTR-YFP and CTR-ChR2 animals (Figure 4a; 48,9% decrease; post-hoc Bonferroni test CTR vs. iuGC-ChR2: t(68) = 2.882, p=0.0317; CTR-YFP vs. iuGC-ChR2: t(68) = 2.78, p=0.0421; CTR-ChR2 vs. iuGC-ChR2: t(68) = 4.141, p=0.0006), with no differences in the number of pellets earned during the test (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Activation of LDT terminals in the VTA during cue exposure period reverted the breakpoint of iuGC animals but had no effect in CTR, CTR-eYFP and CTR-ChR2 animals.
source: Activation of LDT terminals in the VTA during cue exposure period (30 pulses of 15 ms at 20 Hz; around 15 stimulations per session) reverted the breakpoint of iuGC animals but had no effect in CTR, CTR-eYFP and CTR-ChR2 animals (Figure 4a–c; post-hoc Bonferroni test CTR: t(34) = 0.1836, p>0.9999; CTR-ChR2: t(34) = 1.203, p=0.9498; CTR-eYFP: t(34) = 0.5099, p>0.9999; iuGC-ChR2: t(34) = 5.007, p<0.0001;).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4a-c.

claim: If the LDT-VTA optogenetic activation occurred during the inter-trial interval (ITI) period of the test session, it did not revert iuGC-ChR2 motivational deficits.
source: Importantly, if the LDT-VTA optogenetic activation occurred during the inter-trial interval (ITI) period of the test session, it did not revert iuGC-ChR2 motivational deficits (Figure 4b–c; post-hoc Bonferroni: t(34) = 0.5138, p>0.9999), suggesting that LDT-VTA activation elicits a positive behavioral response only when it occurs during specific periods of the test.
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4b-c.

claim: When the number of pulses was increased to 80 pulses of 15 ms at 20 Hz, an increase in the breakpoint of CTR-ChR2 animals was observed.
source: Importantly, when we increased the number of pulses, we observed an increase in the breakpoint of CTR-ChR2 animals (post-hoc Bonferroni: t(22) = 3.666, p=0.0054) when compared to breakpoint of CTR or CTR-eYFP animals (post-hoc Bonferroni CTR-ChR2 vs. CTR: t(44) = 3.075, p=0.0217; CTR-ChR2 vs. CTR-eYFP: t(44) = 3.194, p=0.0156).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2a-b.

claim: LDT-VTA stimulation (30 pulses of 15 ms at 20 Hz every 60 s) elicited conditioning in iuGC group, given by increased preference for the stimulus-associated chamber.
source: LDT-VTA stimulation (30 pulses of 15 ms at 20 Hz every 60 s) elicited conditioning in iuGC group, given by increased preference for the stimulus-associated chamber, ON side, (Figure 4e–f; post-hoc Bonferroni: t(20) = 5.892, p<0.0001), whereas it did not shift preference in CTR and CTR-eYFP animals.
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4e-f.

claim: If the number of stimulus is increased (80 pulses of 15 ms every 15 s), conditioning can be induced in CTR-ChR2 animals.
source: However, if we increase the number of stimulus (80 pulses of 15 ms every 15 s), we were able to induce conditioning in CTR-ChR2 animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 2c; t(8) = 4.737, p=0.0015).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2c.

claim: Stimulation of LDT terminals in the VTA was sufficient to elicit preference for the stimulation-paired chamber in both CTR-ChR2 and iuGC-ChR2 groups in the real-time place preference test.
source: We observed that stimulation of LDT terminals in the VTA was sufficient to elicit preference for the stimulation-paired chamber in both CTR-ChR2 and iuGC-ChR2 groups (Figure 4h; post-hoc Bonferroni CTR-ChR2: t(23) = 8.212, p<0.0001; iuGC-ChR2 t(23) = 8.748, p<0.0001) with no effect on control groups (CTR and CTR-eYFP) (post-hoc Bonferroni CTR: t(23) = 0.1981, p>0.9999; CTR-eYFP: t(23) = 1.784, p>0.9999).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4h.

claim: Prenatal exposure to GCs alters the number of ChAT+ cells in the LDT.
source: Here we show that prenatal exposure to GCs alters the number of ChAT+ cells and induces long-lasting expression changes on cholinergic markers (ChAT and AChE) in the LDT, but had no effect on glutamatergic or GABAergic markers.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: Prenatal exposure to GCs induces long-lasting expression changes on cholinergic markers (ChAT and AChE) in the LDT.
source: Here we show that prenatal exposure to GCs alters the number of ChAT+ cells and induces long-lasting expression changes on cholinergic markers (ChAT and AChE) in the LDT, but had no effect on glutamatergic or GABAergic markers.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: Prenatal exposure to GCs had no effect on glutamatergic or GABAergic markers in the LDT.
source: Here we show that prenatal exposure to GCs alters the number of ChAT+ cells and induces long-lasting expression changes on cholinergic markers (ChAT and AChE) in the LDT, but had no effect on glutamatergic or GABAergic markers.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: Both ChAT and AChE contain a glucocorticoid response element (GRE) in their gene loci.
source: These findings are particularly interesting because both ChAT and AChE contain a glucocorticoid response element (GRE) in their gene loci, pinpointing a direct transcriptional regulation by GCs (Finkelstein et al., 1985; Gilad et al., 1985; Imperato et al., 1989; Berse and Blusztajn, 1997; Battaglia and Ogliari, 2005), although this remains to be confirmed.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: In adulthood iuGC animals present normal basal levels of corticosterone.
source: These cholinergic changes observed in iuGC group are more likely to derive from a new equilibrium set in utero by GC exposure rather than by changes in the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis, since in adulthood iuGC animals present normal basal levels of corticosterone (Blaha and Winn, 1993).

claim: The delay in latency of VTA excitatory responses is not observed upon optical excitation of LDT-VTA terminals, pinpointing to changes in axonal conductivity.

claim: The LDT mediates a divergent excitation/inhibition influence on mesoaccumbens neurons that is likely to excite DAergic cells and inhibit GABA neurons of this region.
source: Importantly, Omelchenko and colleagues suggested that the LDT mediates a divergent excitation/inhibition influence on mesoaccumbens neurons that is likely to excite DAergic cells and inhibit GABA neurons of this region (Omelchenko and Sesack, 2005; Omelchenko and Sesack, 2006); which is in accordance with our data in control animals.

claim: The LDT provides the tonic input necessary for maintaining burst firing of DAergic neurons.
source: The LDT provides the tonic input necessary for maintaining burst firing of DAergic neurons (Lodge and Grace, 2006) and dopamine release to the NAc (Blaha et al., 1996; Forster and Blaha, 2000), contributing to reward behaviors (Lammel et al., 2012; Steidl and Veverka, 2015; Xiao et al., 2016).

claim: Phasic activation of VTA DAergic neurons can induce behavioral conditioning.

Activation of LDT-VTA specific projections shifts animal's preference for the stimulus-associated chamber in both tests.

claim: Pregnant Wistar rats received subcutaneous injections of dexamethasone at 1 mg kg−1 on gestation days 18 and 19 to create the iuGC model.
source: Subcutaneous injections of a synthetic GC, dexamethasone (DEX, Sigma, Germany) at 1 mg kg−1 (iuGC animals) or vehicle (sesame oil, Sigma, Germany; CTR- control animals) were administered on gestation days 18 and 19 (details of the model can be found in Leão et al., 2007; Borges et al., 2013a; Soares-Cunha et al., 2014; Rodrigues et al., 2012; Borges et al., 2013b; Blaha and Winn, 1993).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section describing the animal model.

claim: The iuGC model partially mimics the clinical administration of GCs on women in risk of preterm labour to promote fetal lung maturation.
source: This model, named iuGC (from in utero exposure to GCs) partially mimics the clinical administration of GCs on women in risk of preterm labour (~8% of pregnancies) to promote fetal lung maturation or to manage congenital adrenal hyperplasia during pregnancy.
